📌 Token Approvals: Why an Old "Approve" Can Drain Your Wallet Today

Main Points
⏺ Many dApps ask for permission to spend your tokens before you swap or deposit
⏺ By default, that permission is often unlimited and never expires
⏺ This post explains why old approvals are risky and how to clean them up



1️⃣ Core Idea — An approval lets a smart contract move a specific token from your wallet without asking you again.
2️⃣ Why Unlimited — Apps request "infinite" allowances so you don't pay gas for a new approval every time you trade.
3️⃣ Example — You approved a DEX a year ago. The contract gets exploited today, and the attacker uses your old approval to pull your tokens.
4️⃣ Risk Surface — Phishing sites often ask for an approval instead of a transfer, because many users don't read what they sign.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — Approve only the amount you need, review your allowances regularly with a revoke tool, and remove the ones you no longer use.
Final Thoughts

Your wallet balance is only as safe as the permissions you've handed out. A few minutes of cleanup can close doors you forgot were open.

Japan Boosts Defense Spending, Moves to Turn Its First Carrier Into an F-35B Powerhouse ✈️


Japan is preparing for a major shift in its defense strategy, committing more money to military capabilities and moving ahead with plans to transform its first aircraft carrier to operate U.S.-made F-35B stealth fighters.

The move reflects growing security concerns across the Indo-Pacific, where China’s expanding military presence and North Korea’s missile program have prompted Tokyo to reconsider its long-standing defense posture.

Under its five-year defense program, Japan planned to spend approximately 27 trillion yen, or about $240 billion, marking a significant increase over the previous budget framework. The expansion includes investments in advanced aircraft, naval capabilities, missile defense and other military equipment.

A central part of the plan involves modifying the Izumo-class helicopter destroyer Izumo to accommodate the F-35B, a fifth-generation fighter capable of short takeoffs and vertical landings. The conversion would give Japan a new way to deploy combat aircraft at sea and extend its operational reach beyond traditional land-based airfields.

The F-35B, manufactured by Lockheed Martin, combines stealth technology, advanced sensors and networked combat capabilities. Its ability to operate from relatively short decks makes it particularly valuable for naval forces seeking greater flexibility.

The defense expansion also comes amid pressure from Washington for Japan to purchase more American military equipment and take on a larger role in regional security. Trump had repeatedly called on allies to increase defense spending and address the trade imbalance with the United States.

For Tokyo, the challenge is balancing its security requirements with constitutional restrictions, domestic political considerations and concerns among neighboring countries.

Japan’s evolving military strategy marks a significant development in the Indo-Pacific security landscape, strengthening its ability to respond to regional threats while deepening its defense relationship with Washington.

🌐 Former FBI agent pleads guilty to stealing $2.47M in crypto from 35 investigations 

🔔 Former FBI agent Patrick Steven Yaroch has pleaded guilty to wire fraud and money laundering after stealing approximately $2.47 million in cryptocurrency through nearly 100 unauthorized transfers linked to 35 federal investigations. Yaroch, who previously worked in the bureau’s counterintelligence division, faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. U.S. District Judge Patricia Tolliver Giles accepted his guilty plea in Alexandria, Virginia, with sentencing scheduled for March 4, 2027.

📊 Court documents show that Yaroch worked at the FBI’s Boston Division between 2017 and early 2025, where he was assigned to a squad investigating an adversarial nation-state. He subsequently transferred to the Counterintelligence and Espionage Division in February 2025, gaining access to FBI systems containing cryptocurrency credentials obtained during criminal and intelligence investigations. 

⚡️ Prosecutors said his thefts began no later than December 2024, before he moved to the new division. Using credentials associated with investigations outside his authorized activities, Yaroch accessed cryptocurrency wallets and transferred funds without permission. The approximately 100 fraudulent transactions involved credentials connected to 35 separate FBI investigations. Authorities calculated his total illicit proceeds at $2,474,380.66, substantially exceeding the roughly $1 million initially identified when his activities became public.
